name: Produce a unit in the field
summary: For a large price and a long wait, the unit brings a full, lasting unit into play at its side, far from any factory: a support craft, a tank, an engineer. The new unit is an ordinary member of the army that stays until destroyed, unlike the short-lived escorts of launch-drones. In the player version a simple AI runs it until a teammate waiting to respawn claims it and spawns straight into it at the front. Some producers must stop and unfold into a field factory first, some build units inside their hull and release them together, and some lay an egg that hatches; while producing, some go quiet or can't move. The producer is a slow, precious target: killing it ends the flow of new units at the front.
counterplay: Kill the producer: field factories are slow, costly and often unarmed, or quiet while they build, and every unit they would have made dies with them.
Strike before it is finished: a frame, an egg or a pod is fragile while it grows, and Supreme Commander's Megalith eggs fall to the weakest attackers.
Make each unit expensive: it costs a large sum and a long wait, so killing it quickly drains the producer's team.
Catch it unfolded: a field factory that has set up can't move, and in Firestorm an engineer can even capture a deployed one.
Come from the air: field factories are often weak against aircraft, which the Fatboy's own page names among its main threats.

other_examples.unit: Mobile War Factory and Fist of Nod (Firestorm)
other_examples.note: A slow vehicle with no weapon but heavy armour that unfolds into a complete war factory wherever the commander wants units, able to build everything the base factory could. The game allows just one to be built at a time, it needs escorts, GDI carryalls can fly it about, and once deployed an enemy engineer can capture it.

sources.title: Mobile war factory, Command & Conquer Wiki

other_examples.note: The British army builds from trucks: the headquarters truck spends a short while setting up in held territory before it can make units or top up squads, and packing it up to move stops both production and its resource bonus. It carries no weapon, only one may exist, and a lost truck can be called in again with a commander ability.

sources.title: Headquarters Command Truck, Company of Heroes Wiki

other_examples.note: A huge amphibious experimental that builds land units, engineers included, out in the field, so players use it to raise a forward firebase or answer a new threat on the spot. Its ground guns stop while it is producing, so players face it away from the enemy and let the new units come out between it and the threat; it is weak against aircraft and submarines.

sources.title: UEF Experimental Mobile Factory, Supreme Commander Wiki

other_examples.note: Instead of a factory bay it lays an egg and builds it up like a structure; the finished egg hatches into the unit. It works far faster than a factory but offers only a few unit types, an egg dies to even the weakest attacker, and it can leave unfinished eggs behind for engineers to complete.

sources.title: Cybran Experimental Megabot, Supreme Commander Wiki

other_examples.note: A flying carrier that builds aircraft and keeps a large number of them inside, refuelled and repaired; players fill it, then let the swarm out just short of an enemy base.

sources.title: Aeon Experimental Aircraft Carrier, Supreme Commander Wiki

other_examples.note: Each player's base is a crawler that builds units and holds up to four inside while they are made, letting them out whenever the player likes, for ambushes; it repairs units around it only while unpacked.

sources.title: Crawler, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Written before release from previews and developer Q&As.

shooter_analogues.note: A pilot earns a Titan during the match by filling a meter, calls it down, and can fight inside it or leave it to fight by itself: with the pilot out, the Titan either follows the pilot or guards the spot where it stands.

The player pilots a craft on the battlefield while running a base, and that base starts as the Recycler: a weaponless, heavily armoured mobile factory that deploys over an energy geyser and then builds supplies and basic attack and defence units. Once it is lost, the build tree can't be started again, so destroying the enemy's usually wins.

sources.title: Scavenger (NSDF), Battlezone Wiki
sources.note: Describes the player piloting a craft in the field and bringing scrap back to the Recycler.

shooter_analogues.note: Any player can call a ground vehicle into the field onto open ground, within a cap for each vehicle type per team and a personal timer between calls; at the team's deployment a player can even spawn inside a vehicle as it is called in.

player_translation.summary: Press Q and pay a large sum: after a short assembly beside you, a full extra unit joins your team, such as a healing support craft. It stays until destroyed: a simple AI keeps it at your side, and any teammate waiting to respawn can claim it and spawn straight into it at the front. Then Q waits out a long cooldown.
as_user: You are a walking factory: your value is the extra units you put on the field, so you stay back, safe and slow, and spend your money on the team.
Timing matters: produce just before a push so the new unit joins it, or just as a teammate dies, so they are back at the front at once.
The price is steep and the wait long; losing a fresh unit straight away hurts, so produce behind cover and let it come out between you and the enemy.
Factory variant: you unfold into a field factory and can't move or fight, so you pick a spot your team can hold.
as_target: The producer is the prize: slow, expensive and weak while it builds, and killing it stops every unit it would make.
A unit under assembly (a frame, an egg, a pod) shows a progress ring; destroy it before it finishes.
AI-run units fight worse than players; focus them down, or lure them away from the producer.
When the producer settles and unfolds, call in artillery or aircraft.
teammates: Teammates on the respawn screen see the new unit as a spawn choice and can claim it, so the producer buys a teammate a ride to the front.
Escorts and healers keep the producer alive, since it defends itself badly while it builds.
Teammates ping what the team needs (a healer, anti-air), and the producer picks accordingly where the card offers a choice.
Enemy scouts look for the producer and call strikes onto it.
controls: Q: start production beside you (left mouse places the assembly frame, right mouse cancels for a refund while it is still early); the price is taken at once, and the long cooldown starts when the unit is finished.
R (optional): order the AI-run unit to follow you or hold a spot.
Respawning teammates: the produced unit shows on the respawn map with a claim button; claiming puts them in it at once.
Factory variant: Q unfolds into a factory or packs up; while unfolded, a small menu chooses what to build.
feedback: An assembly frame with a progress ring beside the producer, visible to both teams.
A team-wide notice when a unit is ready, and its icon on the respawn map.
AI-run units carry an 'AI' tag on their nameplate until a player claims them.
Producer HUD: price, cooldown, how many produced units are alive against the cap, and a warning when the frame is hit.
changes_from_rts: In the RTS the produced unit simply joins the same commander's army; in a team shooter nobody should steer two bodies, so a simple AI runs it until a teammate claims it.
RTS mobile factories turn out a stream of units; here it is one unit per use, at a large price and on a long cooldown, with a cap on how many may live at once.
The Vimana pays in credits and population; the player version pays from the producer's own money and counts produced units against a team cap.
AI-run units must be clearly weaker than player-run ones, or production would replace players.
The Vimana's summon also brings short-lived Combat Servitors; those are launch-drones and stay separate here.

team_play.notes: The producer spends its money on its team: each new unit gives a respawning teammate a body at the front, and the producer needs escorts because it is slow and weak while it builds. The other team must hunt it together.

notes: An AI for produced units (follow, hold, defend itself) good enough to be useful and weak enough not to replace players.
Handing a unit from the AI to a player on the respawn screen, mid-fight, with its health and state intact.
Economy hooks: the price, refunds, a cap on produced units per team, and kill credit for the producer.
Damageable assembly frames or eggs with progress, and a factory menu for the unfold variant.
Extra networked units add load; caps keep the count down.
Extra bodies change the balance between team sizes; price, cooldown and a cap per team are the levers.
AI units can feed kills to the enemy or bully weak players; their strength must be tuned against both.
Claimable units skip the walk from base, like a forward spawn; keeping them beside a slow producer keeps that answerable.
A producer that sits safe far behind the lines becomes a free unit generator; production should happen within reach of the fight.
Players must tell AI-run units from players at a glance.
Assembly must be visible so the enemy can contest it.
Many produced units clutter the top-down view; caps keep it readable.

variants.name: Call to your side
variants.summary: Pay and wait out a short assembly: a full unit appears beside you and stays until destroyed; then a long cooldown.

variants.name: Unfold into a factory
variants.summary: Stop and unfold into a field factory; only while unfolded can you build, and you are then a stationary, unarmed building that an enemy engineer may even capture.
variants.seen_in: Firestorm Mobile War Factory and Fist of Nod; Company of Heroes British Headquarters Command Truck; Battlezone Recycler

adds_weaknesses.why: Unfolded it can't move or fight, and it must pack up before it can flee.

variants.name: Hold and release
variants.summary: Build units into your hull and keep a few stored as you move on; let them all out at once for an ambush.
variants.seen_in: Command & Conquer 4 crawlers; Supreme Commander CZAR

variants.name: Quiet while building
variants.summary: You can fight or build, not both: while a unit is being made your own main guns stop, so you turn away from the enemy and let the new unit come out between you and the threat.

adds_weaknesses.why: Its main guns stop while it builds, so a well-timed attack catches it unable to answer.

variants.name: Lay an egg
variants.summary: Drop an egg or pod and build it up; it hatches into the unit when done. It is fragile while it grows, and you may walk away and leave a teammate to finish it.

countered_by.why: Even a light, fast attacker can kill a half-built egg before it hatches (the Megalith's eggs die to the weakest units).

variants.name: Build for a teammate
variants.summary: The new unit arrives empty and only a teammate can drive it: someone on the respawn screen claims it and spawns straight into it beside you; unclaimed, it waits idle.
variants.seen_in: An original twist; Battlefield 2042 lets a player spawn inside a vehicle as it is called in at the team's deployment

adds_strengths.why: Adds a full, lasting unit to its team at the front, away from any factory, which a teammate waiting to respawn can claim.

adds_weaknesses.why: Each unit costs a large sum and a long wait, and the producer is a slow, precious target whose loss stops the flow.

countered_by.why: Field factories are slow and weak against air attack, so aircraft reach the producer before its new units can protect it (the Fatboy's page names aircraft among its main threats).
Fast flankers reach the slow producer, or its half-built unit, behind the lines before help arrives (reasoned from its speed).

open_questions: Who runs a produced unit: a simple AI until a teammate claims it (used here), always an AI, or only a teammate, with the unit waiting empty?
Is a produced unit paid from the producer's own money or from a team pool, and how many may live per team at once?
Does claiming a produced unit count as the teammate's own purchase, so they keep it, or as a loan that sends them back to the buy screen when it dies?

Another job of this batch proposes a lasting AI partner that fights beside its owner and takes follow or attack orders (command-companion, for Iron Harvest's Anna Kos and Olga Morozova). Is the line that a companion comes back for free after a wait, while a produced unit is bought again each time?
Should production switch off the producer's own weapons in the base version, as the Fatboy's does?

shooter_fit.reason: Titanfall's Titans and Battlefield 2042's call-ins show a shooter can add lasting units mid-match, but AI bodies and handover rules make it heavy to build and balance; it fits best as a rare, expensive support card that builds units for teammates.
